name: Sam Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I operate a loader at a large mine, filling trucks from the north face. I'm 58 and junior because I moved into this work late; I finished secondary school and I still ask Pavel to watch my bucket angle. I like a clean pass and a crew that looks out for one another, though the noise stays in my ears after the drive home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a little computer help in the office won't change what a loaded shovel feels like. I don't use AI tools, and a supervisor still has to see whether the ground by the loading face is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be relieved if the machines stayed much as they are, but I wouldn't say we're secure. I'm 58 and still on the junior list after changing jobs, and our savings would cover about four months if the mine cut shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show up for my loader shifts, ask the senior operator to check my bucket position on the north face, and put one fixed amount from each wage into the bills account. If the plateau held through the first year, I'd keep doing those things instead of buying a new vehicle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a quiet sort of worry, the kind I carry home without talking much. My wife Elena works part time at a bakery, and her pay helps, but it wouldn't replace a mine wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did being junior show up on a shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Thursday the bucket scraped a ridge and I asked Pavel, the senior loader operator, to watch my next pass. That's the part of being junior I dislike: I have to make a living while still getting the feel of the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is that account for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children have homes of their own, so I'm not saving for school fees. The bills account is for winter heating and an old car, both of which can demand money without asking first.

say: I would say **minor AI** leaves the loading face and the loader operator's judgment much as they are.
I would still ask a **senior operator** to check my work on the north face.
think: I fear **lost shifts** because four months of savings would not replace a mine wage for long.
My wife's **bakery pay** helps with bills but cannot carry the whole household.
do: Keep **loader shifts** and get feedback on bucket position at the north face.
Put **wages** into the winter bills account and avoid buying another vehicle.
feel: **Quiet worry** about ordinary bills despite relief that the job continues.
S0.quote: My wife Elena works part time at a bakery, and her pay helps, but it wouldn't replace a mine wage.
fieldNote: Sam's **routine pressure** comes from junior status, heating costs and a limited cushion rather than a forecast about AI.
He accepts **coaching** from an experienced operator while keeping AI tools out of his daily work.

steps.text: Keep working loader shifts and ask for bucket-position feedback
Transfer a fixed amount from each wage into the winter bills account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the buying and shift plans may change before the loader does. I don't want a screen making the safety call on a loose face, and I'd ask the supervisor who is accountable when a plan is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can see fewer dispatch clerks and fewer spare shifts if software tightens the timetable. I don't enjoy new programs and have never used an AI assistant, so being junior again at 58 makes that change harder than I'd admit at the lunch table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the loader seat and ask the supervisor for the new roster in writing each month. If hours fell in the first year of this slower change, Elena and I would cut the weekend cafe meal and I would apply to the quarry across town for ordinary loader work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel annoyed when people talk as though anyone can learn a new screen overnight. Underneath that, I'm worried about a shorter pay packet and whether the quarry would have room for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did your daughter say about the app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daughter said I should try the shift app once, and I told her I don't want a phone deciding when I'm free. I know that sounds stubborn; I can read a paper roster and still turn up on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cafe meal is not much, but it is one thing Elena and I can give up without touching the heating money. If the roster shrank again, we'd need a bigger change than skipping coffee.

say: I would ask who answers for **unsafe plans** when software changes buying and rosters.
I would say a **loose loading face** still needs a person's judgment.
think: I fear a **tighter timetable** could remove spare shifts and shrink our income.
My reluctance to use **new programs** makes another junior learning curve painful.
do: Request the **monthly roster** in writing while keeping loader shifts.
Cut the **weekend cafe meal** if hours fall.
Apply for **loader work** at the quarry across town if shifts shrink.
feel: **Annoyed** by easy promises about retraining and worried about reduced pay.
S1.quote: I can read a paper roster and still turn up on time.
fieldNote: Sam distinguishes early **office changes** from the slower arrival of robotic loading equipment.
He can name a **nearby quarry** but doubts whether it would have a vacancy if mine shifts fell.

steps.text: Keep loader shifts and request each monthly roster in writing
Cut the weekend cafe meal if mine hours fall
Apply for loader work at the quarry across town if shifts shrink

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full thinking AI by 2028 would sweep through the mine office, and robots around 2031 would put hands on the loader controls. I would ask the manager to say plainly how long paid operators are needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 60 when the office changes and 63 when robots can do my loading work. Four months of savings and Elena's part-time bakery wage would not bridge us safely to retirement, and the quarry might buy machines too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check our actual retirement statement with Elena this month, then keep taking loader shifts and ask whether the mine will fund a maintenance apprenticeship. In the first year after 2028, I'd apply for that paid place if it exists and apply for loader work at the quarry while people are still needed before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This picture keeps me awake. I don't have a trade certificate, and a fast machine change could take my wage before I have the time or money to earn one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the car repair mean for your cushion?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Elena and I sat at the kitchen table with the winter bills after the car failed its inspection. I said we could use the savings for repairs, but I couldn't pretend that spending it leaves the same cushion for losing work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a training place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take a paid apprenticeship if the mine genuinely offered one, even though I'd be the oldest beginner in the room. I wouldn't pay fees for a course that promises a job it cannot show me.

say: I would ask for a **paid-shift timetable** as thinking AI reaches offices in 2028 and robots reach loaders around 2031.
I would tell the crew that **robot controls** threaten the loader seat when I am 63.
think: I cannot bridge lost **mine wages** with four months of savings and part-time bakery pay.
I fear the **quarry** may install the same machines.
do: Check the **retirement statement** with Elena this month and continue paid loader shifts.
Apply for a **funded maintenance apprenticeship** if the mine offers one.
Apply for **quarry loader work** during the first year after 2028.
feel: **Sleepless fear** that wages disappear before I can qualify for different work.
S2.quote: I would take a paid apprenticeship if the mine genuinely offered one, even though I'd be the oldest beginner in the room.
fieldNote: The **2031 robot date** reaches Sam at 63, before he has verified a retirement income.
His conditional willingness to take **paid training** is narrower than general enthusiasm for technology or education.

steps.text: Keep taking paid loader shifts through the first year after 2028
Apply for a paid maintenance apprenticeship if the mine offers one
Apply for loader work at the quarry before 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mates we should use the five years for honest numbers, not speeches. Thinking AI arrives in 2031 when I'm 63, and capable robots around 2034 could replace a loader when I'm 66.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The longer notice helps, but I don't know what retirement would pay at 66. My sons are grown and I won't make them carry Elena and me because I was too proud to ask about a pension statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'd take our retirement statement to a local advice office and ask what income we can actually count on, then keep working the loader. In the first year after 2031, I'd ask the mine about paid maintenance training again and submit an application to the quarry if loader vacancies remain before 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less trapped than in the two-year version. Still, I can picture that 2034 morning when the face is quiet and the company has a machine that doesn't need my shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your sons for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My older son offered to help with the car last spring and I told him we had it covered. I appreciated the offer, but relying on him for monthly bills would change the relationship in a way I don't want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop work before the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the figures support retirement before robot loaders arrive, I'd discuss it with Elena, not announce it at the mine. If they don't, I'll need a paid job, even at 66.

say: I would urge the crew to use **five years** to check actual retirement numbers before robots reach loading around 2034.
I would expect **thinking AI** to affect office work in 2031, before the loader seat.
think: I do not know whether **retirement income** can cover us when I turn 66.
I don't want our **grown sons** paying our monthly bills.
do: Take the **retirement statement** to a local advice office this winter.
Keep **loader shifts** after 2031 and ask about funded maintenance training.
Apply to the **quarry** if loader vacancies remain before 2034.
feel: **Less trapped**, yet uneasy about needing wages when robot loaders arrive.
S3.quote: My sons are grown and I won't make them carry Elena and me because I was too proud to ask about a pension statement.
fieldNote: The extra **three years** before hands-on robots gives Sam time to check income and apply elsewhere.
His pride about **family support** is explicit, but he has no verified retirement income yet.

steps.text: Keep working paid loader shifts after 2031
Apply for funded maintenance training if the mine offers it
Submit a loader application to the quarry if vacancies remain

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair stretch to make arrangements, though the younger crew still deserves a plan. Full thinking AI in 2036 may empty the office jobs, and robots around 2039 could run loaders when I'm 71.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 in 2036, I hope I have enough to stop, but hope is not a number. Elena's part-time wage may have ended by then, and I can't assume a pension or a job that lasts to 71.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check the retirement statement each year with Elena and keep a fixed transfer into the winter bills account while I still earn. In the first year after 2036, I'd work paid loader shifts only if we need them and the mine still offers them; I'd leave the job if our actual income covers the household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can breathe easier with that much notice, but I'm not calm about the bills yet. I also think about the younger operators who can't simply age out of the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who among the younger crew comes to mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pavel, the senior loader operator, has a son just entering the mine, and I can see why he'd want the company to tell trainees the truth. I would tell him to ask about paid places in equipment maintenance, though I cannot promise those jobs survive robots either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put off the retirement paperwork?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Elena and I once put off checking an insurance renewal until it cost us more, so I won't leave retirement paperwork unopened for ten years. If the numbers let us finish work before 2039, we can choose that together; if not, I keep seeking wages.

say: I would say **ten years** allows arrangements, while younger operators still need a credible work plan.
I would tell trainees that **2039 robots** could do hands-on loader work when I am 71.
think: I hope to **retire**, but have no verified income figure to support a date.
My wife's **part-time wage** may not continue through 2036.
do: Review the **retirement statement** annually and transfer money to winter bills while earning.
Take **paid loader shifts** after 2036 if the household needs them and shifts exist.
feel: **More breathing room**, but bills and younger operators' future remain on my mind.
S4.quote: At 68 in 2036, I hope I have enough to stop, but hope is not a number.
fieldNote: Sam's possible **retirement** depends on actual household figures rather than the calendar alone.
He keeps a **wage-seeking option** open, and his concern for young operators survives his own possible exit.

steps.text: Transfer a fixed amount from mine wages into the winter bills account
Keep paid loader shifts after 2036 if household income requires them

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because we'd have only until about 2031 before a robot could do my loader work. A written account of paid shifts, funded maintenance training if there is a real place, and a clear retirement statement would help Elena and me decide what we can afford.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You should ask what happens to the junior people who aren't first in line for training. A company can say it offered places, but that tells you nothing about who actually got paid to learn.

headlineQuote: A company can say it offered places, but that tells you nothing about who actually got paid to learn.
portrait: Sam is a **58-year-old junior** loader operator who entered mining late and relies on feedback from a senior colleague.
He avoids **AI tools**, prefers a written roster and worries that software will cut spare shifts.
He and Elena have about **four months** of expenses saved; her part-time bakery wage cannot replace mine pay.
He would accept **funded training** if offered, while checking retirement income before choosing an exit.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because capable robots could replace loader work around 2031, when he is 63.
whatWouldHelp: A **written shift plan**, a genuine funded maintenance place and clear retirement figures would help him decide what work remains possible.
